titleText.es: ¡Pero una de las habituales del canal es una chica!
titleText.en: But one of the regulars in the channel is a girl!

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a person-denoting object
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The personal a also appears before words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) when they directly receive an action, even though they do not identify one specific individual.

example.en: I did not see anyone.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: as (in the role or capacity of)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the role, identity, or point of view from which someone speaks or acts. This is different from cómo with an accent, which asks “how.”

example.en: As a doctor, I recommend resting.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish uses a form of estar, rather than ser, to say where someone or something is. Estoy is the form for the speaker.

example.en: I am at home.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Visitó is a completed-past form of visitar for he, she, or formal you. The written accent distinguishes it from visito, “I visit.”

example.en: Marta visited the museum yesterday.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In online chat, canal names a shared conversation space or channel, not a television station or waterway.

example.es: Nos vemos en el canal del grupo.
example.en: See you in the group's channel.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Pidiendo is the ongoing-action form of pedir. The e in pedir changes to i before the -iendo ending: pedir becomes pidiendo.

example.en: She came in asking for help.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hecho is the irregular completed-action form of hacer, “to do” or “to make.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “done.”

example.en: I have already done the homework.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to it; marks the thing receiving the effect
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Le can appear before a verb even when a later phrase beginning with a names the receiver explicitly. English normally states that receiver only once.

example.es: Le cambié la rueda al coche.
example.en: I changed the car's wheel.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Nick is an informal English loan used in Spanish online communities for a nickname or username.

example.es: Uso otro nick en ese foro.
example.en: I use another username on that forum.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Femenino is masculine singular here because it describes the masculine word nick.

example.en: She chose a feminine name.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Entrar literally means to enter. With a group or online space, it can describe joining or coming into that community.

example.es: Ana entra en el chat cada tarde.
example.en: Ana joins the chat every afternoon.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en broma, “as a joke”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: En combines with broma to make the fixed expression en broma. Translating en by itself as “in” would be unnatural here.

example.en: I said it as a joke.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: joke; completes en broma, “as a joke”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Broma means a joke. After en, the complete expression describes something done jokingly rather than seriously.

example.en: It was only a joke.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: her; to her (marks the female recipient)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Le identifies the person who receives a request or another action. The same Spanish form can also mean “to him” or formal “to you”; context identifies the person.

example.en: I asked Marta for water.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Pedir is used when requesting a thing or action. Preguntar is normally used instead when asking a question.

example.en: You ask the waiter for the bill.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: naked (feminine singular; describing an implied woman)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Desnuda is feminine singular. Here it describes the understood woman rather than the plural word fotos, so English expresses the relationship differently.

example.es: La modelo aparece desnuda en el cuadro.
example.en: The model appears naked in the painting.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Siendo is the irregular ongoing-action form of ser, “to be.” It can follow a form of estar to describe current behavior.

example.en: You are being very kind.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Gilipollas is a strong informal insult widely associated with Spain. It can keep the same form for a man or a woman.

example.en: Don't be a jerk.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: making someone laugh very hard; literally “killing” (in matar de risa)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Matando normally means “killing.” In matar de risa, it is part of an idiom for causing intense laughter.

example.es: Ese cómico me está matando de risa.
example.en: That comedian is making me laugh so hard.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; links matar to risa in matar de risa
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The de is required by the fixed expression matar de risa, which means to make someone laugh very hard.

example.es: La historia nos mató de risa.
example.en: The story made us laugh really hard.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Risa means laughter. In matar de risa it completes a fixed expression for making someone laugh intensely.

example.en: Her comment made me laugh.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; part of la razón por la que, “the reason why”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish uses por before la que to connect a stated reason with the following explanation. Natural English normally uses “why.”

example.es: Esa es la razón por la que vine.
example.en: That is the reason why I came.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Escasas describes a feminine plural group as limited in number or difficult to find.

example.en: Tickets are scarce.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Parte can mean a physical part or, more broadly, a portion or area of a place or system.

example.es: Conozco varias partes de la ciudad.
example.en: I know several parts of the city.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: you frequent; you regularly visit or use
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Frecuentar means to go to or use a place regularly. Frecuentas is the present form for informal singular you.

example.en: Do you frequent this library?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces the person who likes something
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With gustar, a can introduce or clarify the person experiencing the liking. A quien means “to whom” in the Spanish structure even when natural English simply says “who likes.”

example.es: Es una amiga a quien le gusta bailar.
example.en: She is a friend who likes dancing.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Unaccented quien refers back to a person in a statement. After a preposition such as a, natural English often uses “who” rather than formal “whom.”

example.es: La persona con quien trabajo es amable.
example.en: The person I work with is kind.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: marks the person whose preference or reaction is described
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With gustar and similar preference expressions, le identifies the person experiencing the liking, appeal, or reaction. The thing that causes that reaction controls whether the verb is singular or plural, while le stays the same.

example.es: A Luis le gustan los trenes.
example.en: Luis likes trains.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: are liked; appeal (used with plural liked things)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Gustan is plural because the things liked are plural. The person who likes them is identified separately by me, te, le, nos, os, or les.

example.en: I like these songs.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Friki is an informal Spanish description borrowed from English “freak.” It can be a noun for a geek or an adjective for geeky interests or people; here it describes a plural group.

example.en: We love geeky movies.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Banear is an informal internet verb formed from English “ban.” The ending te is attached to the unchanged -ar form and identifies informal singular you as the person banned.

example.es: El moderador puede banearte del foro.
example.en: The moderator can ban you from the forum.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: is; is located (inside a relative description)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hay normally means “there is” or “there are.” Inside a description with que, natural English can instead use “is,” as in la mesa que hay aquí, “the table that is here.”

example.es: La tienda que hay junto al banco cierra tarde.
example.en: The shop next to the bank closes late.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Detrás is followed by de before the person or thing used as the reference point.

example.es: El jardín está detrás de la casa.
example.en: The garden is behind the house.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; completes detrás de, “behind”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Use de after detrás and before the reference point. The two words work together as detrás de.

example.es: La mochila está detrás de mí.
example.en: The backpack is behind me.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; marks llamarse, “to be called”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Llamarse uses a matching small word: me llamo, te llamas, se llama, nos llamamos, and so on. With he, she, formal you, or one named thing, use se.

example.en: Her name is Inés.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: With se, llama is a form of llamarse used to state a person's or thing's name. Without se, llama can instead mean “calls.”

example.en: My dog is called Coco.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Asignada is the completed-action form of asignar used as a description. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular person or thing.

example.en: I have an assigned table.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Intenta tells one person addressed informally to try something. The same written form can mean “he, she, or formal you tries” in a statement; context marks it as a command here.

example.en: Try to open the door.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Conectarte combines conectar in its unchanged -ar form with te, which identifies informal singular you. Conectarse a Internet commonly means to connect or go online.

example.en: You can log on from home.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to; required before what someone connects to
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Conectarse normally takes a before the network, service, or device being joined.

example.en: I connect to the network.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: marks you as the affected owner; English often uses “your”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish can identify an affected owner with me, te, le, nos, or les and still use el or la before the owned thing. English often uses a possessive instead: te rompieron el móvil means “they broke your phone.”

example.en: I cleaned your computer.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Freirá is the future form of freír for he, she, or formal you. With electronics, freír can figuratively mean to destroy or burn out the device.

example.es: El exceso de voltaje freirá el circuito.
example.en: The excess voltage will fry the circuit.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: With estar, bueno or buena can informally describe a person as physically attractive. This use can sound objectifying, so it is not a neutral substitute for guapo or guapa in every setting.

example.es: Dice que esa actriz está muy buena.
example.en: He says that actress is really hot.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dispara tells one person addressed informally to fire a weapon or shoot. The same form can mean “he, she, or formal you fires” in a statement.

example.en: Aim and fire.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: Why can Spanish use le or les with a verb and then still name the receiver with a phrase beginning with a?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use le or les with the verb, and use a plus the noun or person to identify the receiver explicitly.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Le is for one receiver and les for more than one. It normally appears before a conjugated verb, but it can attach to an unchanged verb form, as in darle. The later a phrase clarifies who or what the short marker refers to; Spanish often keeps both pieces even though natural English states the receiver only once.

example.en: I gave the dog water.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is said or done as a joke rather than seriously?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use en broma after the action.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: En broma is a fixed expression meaning “as a joke” or “jokingly.” Its opposite is en serio, “seriously.”

example.en: I said it to you as a joke.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something makes a person laugh extremely hard?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of matar, then de risa, and identify the person who laughs.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is an exaggerated fixed expression: matar literally means “to kill,” but matar de risa means to make someone laugh very hard. The person can appear as me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, or las, or after the personal a.

example.es: Ese vídeo nos mató de risa.
example.en: That video made us laugh so hard.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can razón introduce why something happened?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use razón por la que, meaning “reason why.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Razón is normally accompanied by a determiner or description, as in la razón or una razón. With a plural reason, use razones por las que. Spanish literally builds “reason for which,” while natural English normally says “reason why.”

example.es: Esa es la razón por la que salí temprano.
example.en: That is the reason why I left early.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone likes one thing or several things?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person; then use gusta for one liked thing and gustan for more than one.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish builds this as if the liked thing is pleasing to the person. The liked thing controls the verb: gusta este libro but gustan estos libros. You can clarify the person with a phrase beginning with a, such as a Marta or a quien.

example.es: A Marta le gustan los gatos.
example.en: Marta likes cats.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something is behind a person or object?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use detrás de before the person or object used as the reference point.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Keep de after detrás. Before a pronoun, use forms such as detrás de mí, detrás de ti, or detrás de él; do not use the subject forms yo or tú after de.

example.es: El coche está detrás de la casa.
example.en: The car is behind the house.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you state what a person or thing is called?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun and a form of llamar, then give the name: me llamo, te llamas, se llama, and so on.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The dictionary form is llamarse. The small pronoun changes with the person: me llamo means “I am called,” te llamas is informal “you are called,” and se llama is used for he, she, formal you, or one named thing.

example.en: The cat is called Luna.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: tener + objeto + participio que describe su estado
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that you have a person or thing in an assigned, prepared, closed, or other resulting state?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of tener, name or replace the object, and add its completed-action form as a description.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The completed-action form is often called a past participle. Here it behaves like a describing word and matches the object: tengo la puerta cerrada, but tengo los documentos preparados. This differs from haber plus a participle, where the participle does not change.

example.en: I have the tables reserved.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: conectarse a Internet / a una red
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone connects to the internet or a network?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of conectarse, then a before Internet, la red, or the service being joined.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Conectarse uses me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match the person connecting. Keep a before the destination: me conecto a la red, te conectas a Internet. In an unchanged verb form, the small pronoun attaches to the end, as in conectarte.

example.es: Nos conectamos a Internet por la mañana.
example.en: We connect to the internet in the morning.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What can estar bueno or estar buena mean when it informally describes a person?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: It can mean that the person is physically attractive or “hot.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Use está bueno for a masculine singular person and está buena for a feminine singular person; other forms change for number and speaker. This informal use focuses on physical appearance and can sound objectifying, so guapo or guapa is often a more neutral compliment.

example.es: En la película dicen que el actor está muy bueno.
example.en: In the movie they say the actor is really hot.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: a fictional electromagnetic-pulse weapon meant to disable electronics
cardDefinitions.noteEn: PEM abbreviates pulso electromagnético, the Spanish term for EMP. A strong electromagnetic pulse can disrupt or damage electronic equipment; the comic turns that idea into a portable enforcement weapon.

applications.explanationEn: Estoy is the speaker's form of estar, and aquí supplies the location, so this is a location use rather than an identity use of ser.
The -iendo form presents the requesting as an action happening during the visit.

regions.labelEs: ¿QUÉ LE HAS HECHO A MI PUERTA?

applications.explanationEn: Has is the present helper for informal singular you, and hecho is hacer's irregular completed-action form.

applications.exampleEs: LE HAS HECHO A MI PUERTA
applications.explanationEn: Le marks the affected receiver before the verb, while a mi puerta explicitly clarifies what le refers to.

regions.labelEs: CUANDO ALGUIEN CON UN NICK FEMENINO ENTRA EN TU COMUNIDAD, Y DICES "ANDA, UNA MUJER EN INTERNET", Y "EN BROMA" LE PIDES FOTOS DESNUDA, ESTÁS SIENDO UN GILIPOLLAS. NO ESTÁS SIENDO IRÓNICO. NO ESTÁS MATANDO DE RISA A NADIE. ERES LA PRIMERA RAZÓN POR LA QUE LAS MUJERES SON TAN ESCASAS EN INTERNET.

applications.explanationEn: En and broma form the fixed manner expression indicating that the request is framed as joking rather than serious.
Estás matches the listener, and siendo supplies the behavior presented as currently in progress.
Estás again matches the listener, while siendo presents the described behavior as what is happening now.
Estás matches informal singular you, and matando supplies the ongoing action with its -ando ending.
Matando de risa supplies the fixed exaggerated laughter expression, and a nadie identifies the negated person who would experience it.

applications.exampleEs: NO ESTÁS MATANDO DE RISA A NADIE
applications.explanationEn: No remains before the verb phrase because nadie follows it; the two negative words reinforce one negative meaning in Spanish.
A marks nadie as the person directly affected by the laughter expression, even though nobody is negated.
Razón names the cause being discussed, and por la que introduces the following explanation with a feminine form that matches razón.

regions.labelEs: AL MENOS, LAS PARTES QUE TÚ FRECUENTAS.

applications.explanationEn: Al menos narrows the claim to its minimum defensible scope.
Frecuentas already identifies informal singular you, so the printed tú adds pointed contrast and emphasis.

regions.labelEs: COMO ALGUIEN A QUIEN LE GUSTAN LAS CHICAS FRIKIS, NO APRECIO ESTAS COSAS. ESTOY AQUÍ PARA BANEARTE DE INTERNET. LA CHICA QUE HAY DETRÁS DE MÍ CON EL CAÑÓN PEM SE LLAMA JOANNA. LA TIENES ASIGNADA PARA EL PRÓXIMO AÑO. INTENTA CONECTARTE A INTERNET Y TE FREIRÁ EL PC.

applications.exampleEs: A QUIEN LE GUSTAN LAS CHICAS FRIKIS
applications.explanationEn: A quien and le identify the person experiencing the liking, while gustan is plural because las chicas frikis is a plural liked group.
Estoy is the speaker's form of estar, and aquí supplies the location.
Para introduces the purpose, and banear remains in its unchanged dictionary form inside banearte.
Detrás de gives the relative location, and mí is the required pronoun form after the preposition de.
Se matches the woman being named, and llama is the corresponding form of llamarse before her printed proper name.
La replaces the already identified woman and appears directly before the finite verb tienes.
La is the feminine object, tienes supplies tener, and asignada uses its feminine ending to describe that object's resulting assigned state.
Intenta is the positive command used for one person addressed informally.
Intenta is the command to try, while conectar remains in its unchanged -ar form and carries the attached pronoun te.
Conectarte attaches te to the unchanged verb form for the listener, and a introduces the network being joined.
Está supplies the current-state form, and buena is feminine singular because the speaker is informally judging a woman as physically attractive.

excludedUnits.rationale: Joanna is a person's proper name retained unchanged, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Dispara is the positive command used for one person addressed informally.
